questions.q: The astrologer sat under a spreading ________ tree in the Town Hall Park.
His forehead was resplendent with sacred ash and ________.
He had a working analysis of mankind's troubles: marriage, money and the tangles of ________.
Guru Nayak's village was two days' journey due ________ of the town.
The astrologer told Guru Nayak that his enemy had been crushed under a ________.
As a youngster, the astrologer drank, gambled and ________ badly one day.
Fill in the blank: She ________ (study) for her exams for three hours. (present perfect continuous)
Fill in the blank: By the time we arrived, they ________ (wait) for us for over an hour.
Fill in the blank: The children ________ (play) in the garden since morning.
Fill in the blank: She realised she ________ (work) on the wrong assignment all night.
Use the right phrasal verb (put by / put out / look after): Every wise person ________ a little money for a rainy day.
Correct the verb: At the beginning of the year, Rahul did not knew a word of Urdu.
Correct the verb: The negative factors at home causes all these differences.
Describe the astrologer's appearance and how it attracted customers.
questions.answer: His forehead shone with sacred ash and vermilion, dark whiskers streamed down his cheeks and he wore a saffron turban. These made his searching eyes look prophetic, and people were drawn to him like bees to flowers.

questions.q: How did the astrologer manage to satisfy his clients?
questions.answer: He let each client talk for ten minutes, which gave him material for many answers. He then spoke of common troubles — marriage, money, human ties — and flattered them, so nine out of ten agreed with him.

questions.q: How did the astrologer know so much about Guru Nayak's past?
questions.answer: He was the man who had stabbed Guru Nayak in a drunken quarrel and pushed him into a well. So he knew about the knife, the well and even the name, though Guru Nayak thought it was astrology.

questions.q: Why did the astrologer advise Guru Nayak to go home and never travel south again?
questions.answer: He wanted to keep Guru Nayak far away from the town where he lived, so that Guru Nayak would stop searching for his attacker and the astrologer's secret would stay safe.

questions.q: What is the significance of the title 'An Astrologer's Day'?
questions.answer: The story follows one day in the astrologer's life, from setting up at noon to going home at midnight. That single day brings the meeting with Guru Nayak, which frees him from years of guilt.

questions.q: What made the astrologer's wife happy, and what worried her?
questions.answer: She was overjoyed with the twelve and a half annas, as she could buy jaggery and coconut to make sweets for their child. But she noticed her husband looked worried and was shocked to learn he had once tried to kill a man.

questions.q: Why did the astrologer shiver when confronted by the stranger?
questions.answer: When the stranger lit his cheroot, the astrologer saw his face by the match-light and recognised Guru Nayak, the man he had stabbed and pushed into a well years ago. He feared he would be recognised and punished, so he shivered in his grip and his voice grew faint.

questions.q: Why is the ending of 'An Astrologer's Day' a surprise? How does Narayan prepare for it?
questions.answer: We learn only at the end that the astrologer himself had stabbed Guru Nayak, which explains his fear, his knowledge and his advice. Narayan prepares for it with hints: the astrologer left his village suddenly, he feels uneasy when he sees the stranger's face, and he tries to return the anna and leave.

questions.q: Bring out the irony in the story.
questions.answer: The astrologer knows nothing of the stars yet is trusted as a prophet. He calls Guru Nayak a 'swine' who cheated him of a rupee, though he has deceived Guru Nayak completely. And the 'prediction' that freed Guru Nayak was really a confession that freed the astrologer.

or.q: Write a character sketch of the astrologer.
or.answer: He is shrewd and observant, reading people's worries from their talk and faces. He is a fake but hard-working, earning an honest man's wage by his wits. He carries guilt for a crime of his youth, and he is quick-witted under pressure, turning danger into safety and relief.

questions.q: How is the contrast of light and darkness used in the story?
questions.answer: The park has no municipal lights; the half-light hides the astrologer's ignorance and his identity. A match-light reveals Guru Nayak's face to him, a moment of recognition. At the end the green shaft of light vanishes, leaving darkness, as his secret stays hidden — yet he himself is relieved.
